title: Why Small Heat Pumps Beat Large Ones on SCOP
author: Heat Pump Database
summary: Our data shows residential ASHPs between 4-20kW post noticeably higher SCOP than commercial units above 20kW - even when refrigerant and test conditions are matched. Here's what's actually driving the gap.
body_html:
Anyone who spends time in the Visualise section of this database will have noticed the same thing: plot SCOP against maximum heating capacity, and there's a visible step down once you cross roughly 20kW. Products in the 4–20kW band, which covers most UK homes, cluster noticeably higher than the commercial-scale units above it. We dug into the underlying data to find out whether that's a real effect or an artefact of how the chart is drawn, and if real, why it happens.

The pattern holds up under scrutiny

The naive comparison (every product with a published SCOP, split at 20kW) shows a modest gap: 4.79 average SCOP for 4–20kW products versus 4.64 for those above 20kW. That's real but small, and it's diluted by mixing heat pump types: ground and water source units, which behave differently from air source, are unevenly distributed between the two bands.

Once we control for that, looking only at air source heat pumps tested at the same flow-temperature condition (SCOP at W35, the standard EN 14825 basis), the gap widens substantially: 4.68 average SCOP for 4–20kW ASHPs, versus 3.92 for those above 20kW. That's a 15–20% relative difference, and it holds within every major refrigerant type we checked:

Refrigerant4-20kW mean SCOP>20kW mean SCOP

R2904.874.16
R410A4.213.69

So it isn't simply that small heat pumps happen to use a more efficient refrigerant blend. Something else is going on.

It's really a residential-vs-commercial split

The clearest signal in the data is who's making these products. In the 4–20kW band, 94% of listings are residential units, dominated by brands like Daikin, Panasonic, LG, Riello and Baxi. Above 20kW, 98% are commercial units, dominated by HVAC specialists like Rhoss, Swegon, Clivet, Carrier and Trane. These are almost entirely disjoint markets, and that matters more than the capacity number itself.

Residential ASHPs compete on SCOP because it's tied directly to UK policy: MCS listing, SAP calculations and Boiler Upgrade Scheme eligibility all hinge on the published figure. Commercial equipment isn't sold against the same yardstick, so there's less commercial pressure to optimise for it.

Modulation, not just marketing

Most small residential ASHPs use a single variable-speed inverter compressor that can turn down to a small fraction of its rated output. SCOP is a seasonal average dominated by part-load conditions, mild autumn and spring days rather than the coldest day of the year, so a compressor that modulates smoothly down low is exactly what the metric rewards.

Larger commercial systems more often reach their capacity by staging multiple compressors on and off rather than continuously modulating one, which is a sensible way to guarantee output for a building but tends to be less efficient at partial load, precisely the condition SCOP weights most heavily.

Two explanations we ruled out

Before settling on the above, we checked two obvious alternatives:

Are the big units just working harder, with higher flow temperatures? No. If anything, the 4–20kW band has a slightly higher average maximum flow temperature (67°C vs 60°C), which should hurt their SCOP relative to the larger units, not help it.

Is this just a reporting gap: do fewer large commercial products even publish SCOP? Partly, but not enough to explain it. 73% of 4–20kW products in the database list an SCOP figure, versus 63% of those above 20kW: a real gap consistent with SCOP being a residential/policy-driven metric, but far too small on its own to account for a 0.7-point difference in the average.

The takeaway

If you're comparing a domestic-scale heat pump against something plumbed for a larger building, don't expect the SCOP figures to be comparable on the same terms: they're drawn from different markets with different design priorities and different regulatory pressure. For sizing a home, the 4–20kW figures in this database remain the fair like-for-like comparison; for commercial specification, capacity, reliability and total installed cost typically matter more than chasing the last point of seasonal efficiency.

Sources & further reading

The mechanisms behind this gap (part-load behaviour, compressor modulation and the different regulatory pressure on residential versus commercial equipment) are corroborated by independent industry and technical sources:

  • Lochinvar – “SCOP vs COP: What Engineers, Specifiers, and M&E Contractors Need to Know for Commercial Decarbonisation Projects”, on why SCOP carries different weight and regulatory drivers in commercial specification than in the residential market.
  • IDM Energie – “Part-Load Operation in Heat Pumps”, explaining why modulating systems achieve higher seasonal efficiency because COP improves at part load, and buildings spend most of their time there.
  • IDM Energie – “EN 14825 Standard: Heat Pump Seasonal Performance Testing”, on how the standard this database’s SCOP figures are drawn from explicitly weights part-load performance rather than a single full-load point.
  • HVAC Know It All – “Variable Speed Scroll Compressors: Why They Dominate Modern Heat Pumps”, on why continuously modulating compressors outperform staged/cycling designs at part load, the operating pattern more common in larger commercial units.

tldr: Small heat pumps (4–20kW) post meaningfully higher SCOP than large commercial units, mainly because residential kit is optimised for SCOP and uses modulating compressors, while commercial systems stage multiple compressors and aren't benchmarked the same way.

title: Who Really Owns Your Heat Pump? Mapping the Parent Companies
author: Heat Pump Database
summary: 77 manufacturers in this database collapse into a much smaller set of corporate parents. We mapped which brands share an owner, including two ownership changes that only completed in the last two months.
image_credit: Heat Pump Database, brand ownership map showing 8 parent groups and 19 subsidiary brands
tldr: Eight corporate groups own 19 of the 77 heat pump brands in this database between them. The biggest recent moves: Carrier sold Riello to Ariston Group in July 2026, and Bosch absorbed Johnson Controls' York and Hitachi lines in January 2026.
body_html:
Scroll through the manufacturers list on this site and it reads like 77 independent companies. In practice, a chunk of that list collapses into a much smaller set of corporate parents, several of which have reshuffled their heat pump brands within the last 18 months. Below are the ownership links we could confirm from company announcements and filings, focused only on the parents and subsidiaries that are both represented in this database.

Two of these groups changed hands within the last two months of this article being published: Riello moved from Carrier to Ariston Group on 1 July 2026, and Bosch finished absorbing Johnson Controls’ York and Hitachi lines in January 2026. Ownership in this industry moves fast, so treat this as a snapshot rather than a permanent map.

Carrier Global Corporation

Carrier owns Carrier and CIAT outright, and completed its acquisition of Viessmann’s Climate Solutions business, the heat pump and boiler side of the company, in January 2024 for around €12 billion. Carrier also holds the rights to sell Toshiba-branded heat pumps across Europe under a separate licensing arrangement with Toshiba Corporation, which otherwise remains independent. Riello was part of this group until Carrier sold it to Ariston Group in July 2026.

Ariston Group

Ariston and Riello are now siblings: Ariston Group completed its purchase of Riello’s heating and heat pump business from Carrier on 1 July 2026, for gross proceeds of around $440 million.

Vaillant Group

Vaillant and Glow-worm sit under the same German family-owned group. Glow-worm is part of Vaillant’s “Saunier Duval Brand Group” alongside Saunier Duval and Protherm, neither of which are stocked in this database.

Groupe Atlantic

Atlantic, Ideal Heating and Clade are all Groupe Atlantic brands, alongside Gledhill, Hamworthy and Keston, which aren’t in this database. Groupe Atlantic itself was recently majority-acquired by Paloma Rheem Holdings.

NIBE Group

Nibe, CTC and Rhoss are all NIBE Industrier AB brands: CTC came with the 2016–17 acquisition of Enertech Group, and Rhoss became a wholly-owned NIBE subsidiary in January 2019 after NIBE bought out the remaining stake from the Bellò family.

Bosch Home Comfort Group

This is the newest and largest cluster here. Bosch completed its purchase of Johnson Controls’ residential and light-commercial HVAC business, including the Johnson Controls–Hitachi joint venture, with the integration finishing in January 2026. Bosch, York and Hitachi (for residential and light-commercial units) now share one parent.

Johnson Controls

Johnson Controls kept its industrial refrigeration and heat pump business when it sold the residential side to Bosch, so Sabroe remains a Johnson Controls brand, just a smaller one than before.

Midea Group

Midea holds an 80% stake in Clivet, acquired in 2016; the Bellò family that founded Clivet retained the remaining 20%.

What this means if you're comparing quotes

None of this means sibling brands are identical products with different badges; Carrier, CIAT and Viessmann heat pumps, for instance, are built to different specifications and sold through different channels. But it's worth knowing when two quotes you're comparing ultimately report to the same boardroom, particularly for warranty terms, parts availability and who you're actually negotiating with if you push back on price.
